paragraphs: An intervention can affect different people differently, so its overall average effect may conceal important variation. Conditional Average Treatment Effects, or CATE, describe how average effects vary with observed characteristics. Many methods for estimating them assume that all factors influencing both treatment and outcome have been measured. The paper addresses situations where that assumption may fail.

The authors propose a general framework that uses instrumental variables to estimate CATE in the possible presence of an unmeasured confounder. This changes how the analysis addresses hidden influences instead of simply assuming them away. The problem also matters in randomized trials with noncompliance, where assigned treatment and received treatment may differ.

Alongside the framework, the authors construct estimators with improved efficiency and robustness across various forms of model misspecification. Simulations and a real-data example demonstrate the framework's efficacy. The contribution is an approach to estimating differences in treatment effects while explicitly accommodating possible hidden confounding and examining robustness when modeling choices are imperfect.
neurips-2024-a-non-parametric-direct-lea.tldr: The paper uses instrumental variables to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with possible unmeasured confounding, developing more efficient and robust estimators.

paragraphs: A model can recognize an animal partly by its background rather than by the animal itself. Tests of such misleading associations often target shortcuts found in ImageNet-trained models. The paper asks whether CLIP's strong performance on those tests adequately reveals shortcuts associated with its own training data.

The authors construct CounterAnimal by grouping animal photographs according to their backgrounds. For each animal class, they identify two groups between which a CLIP model's performance drops substantially. This makes the benchmark sensitive to realistic background associations that conventional tests may miss. Evaluations show that these associations affect CLIP models with different architectures and pretraining data, while having limited influence on ImageNet models.

The paper also provides theoretical insights indicating that CLIP's training objective cannot itself supply additional robustness. Its experiments nevertheless find that larger models and higher-quality pretraining data help reduce the problem. The findings make robustness evaluation more specific: success against one model family's shortcuts does not establish resistance to the shortcuts learned by another.
neurips-2024-a-sober-look-at-the-robustn.tldr: CounterAnimal reveals background shortcuts shared across CLIP models, showing why ImageNet-oriented tests can give an incomplete picture of their robustness.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through a sequence of steps that move from high noise toward a finished result. Guidance is used to improve generation, commonly with the same strength throughout that sequence. This paper investigates whether applying guidance at every stage is actually useful.

The authors find a distinct pattern: guidance harms generation at the high-noise beginning, contributes little near the low-noise end, and helps in the middle. They therefore activate it only within a selected interval of noise levels. This changes when guidance operates, making its timing an additional control over the generation process.

Restricting guidance improves both inference speed and output quality in the reported experiments. On ImageNet-512, the reported record FID improves from 1.81 to 1.40. The authors find quantitative and qualitative benefits across sampler settings, network architectures, and datasets, including Stable Diffusion XL. These findings motivate exposing the guidance interval as a configurable hyperparameter so that users can adjust where guidance contributes during sampling.
neurips-2024-applying-guidance-in-a-limi.tldr: Applying diffusion guidance only at intermediate noise levels improves generation quality and speed across the settings studied.

paragraphs: Time series and language both arrive as ordered sequences, making language models a potential foundation for forecasting. AutoTimes builds on that similarity while explicitly using the autoregressive behavior of decoder-only language models: predictions are generated sequentially, extending the sequence over multiple steps.

The method maps time-series data into the embedding space used for language tokens. It supports arbitrary prediction lengths, flexible amounts of past input, and compatibility with any decoder-only language model. It also treats time series as prompts, allowing information beyond the immediate lookback window to contribute to forecasting. Textual timestamps represented through the language model help align multiple time series chronologically.

The authors report state-of-the-art forecasting performance with 0.1% trainable parameters and more than fivefold training and inference speedups relative to advanced language-model-based forecasters. They also report scalability with larger language models. The contribution is a way to adapt language models' existing sequential generation capabilities to forecasting while retaining flexibility in both input context and forecast length.
neurips-2024-autotimes-autoregressive-ti.tldr: AutoTimes adapts decoder-only language models for flexible autoregressive forecasting, reporting strong accuracy with few trainable parameters and faster computation.

paragraphs: Diffusion planning generates trajectories that describe how a decision-making process could unfold over a long horizon. Although these trajectories can be high quality, producing them through repeated sampling is expensive. That cost limits how frequently a system can make a new decision, creating a practical obstacle for fast planning.

DiffuserLite introduces a planning refinement process that develops trajectories from coarse descriptions into finer detail. The framework reduces the modeling of redundant information through this progression. Its central design choice connects the amount of trajectory detail being generated to the computational work required, aiming to preserve useful planning capability while increasing decision frequency.

The reported experiments achieve 122.2 decisions per second, or 112.7 times the frequency of predominant frameworks, alongside state-of-the-art performance on D4RL, Robomimic, and FinRL. The authors also describe DiffuserLite as a plugin for accelerating other diffusion planners. The results support coarse-to-fine refinement as a useful structural approach to making diffusion-based decision making faster.
neurips-2024-diffuserlite-towards-real-t.tldr: DiffuserLite refines trajectories from coarse to fine detail, reporting much faster diffusion planning and state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Multi-objective optimization seeks solutions that balance competing goals according to a person's preferences. A difficulty arises when an optimizer follows an inaccurate reward model: it can pursue solutions that score well without matching what the person wants. Human feedback also varies, making preference learning uncertain.

This paper proposes using human comparisons directly through a clustering-based stochastic dueling bandit algorithm. The algorithm organizes the comparison problem into clusters and learns from uncertain feedback without requiring a predefined reward model or extensive model selection. Its stated regret bound is O(K² log T), where K counts clusters and T counts rounds.

The learned preferences are converted into a common probabilistic representation that existing evolutionary multi-objective algorithms can use. The framework also supplies a stopping criterion intended to manage computational resources and the burden of requesting human judgments. Experiments across 48 benchmark problems, including RNA inverse design and protein structure prediction, demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution links preference elicitation, optimization, and stopping decisions within one framework.
neurips-2024-direct-preference-based-evo.tldr: The framework guides multi-objective optimization with uncertain human comparisons, using clustered dueling bandits and a principled stopping criterion.

paragraphs: Many models begin with pretraining and are then fine-tuned for separate tasks. Combining their weights could produce a shared model with several capabilities, but existing merging methods often lose performance or require extra data and training. This paper identifies a central difficulty: one fixed set of weights struggles to reproduce every specialized model's behavior.

EMR-Merging addresses this by pairing a unified model with very lightweight task-specific modulators. It first elects unified weights from the available model weights. It then generates masks and rescalers that align the unified model with each task-specific model in direction and magnitude, respectively. Task-specific adjustments therefore remain part of the merged system.

The method requires neither additional training nor access to data for tuning. The authors report strong performance against existing merging methods across vision, language, parameter-efficient fine-tuned models, and multimodal models, including settings with up to 30 vision models. The findings support lightweight modulation as a practical way to retain task specialization within a shared model.
neurips-2024-emr-merging-tuning-free-hig.tldr: EMR-Merging combines unified model weights with lightweight task-specific masks and rescalers, requiring no tuning data or additional training.

paragraphs: People can learn categories and relationships from only a few images. This paper investigates which pretrained neural-network representations best predict how that learning unfolds. The authors compare 86 models with human learning trajectories in two tasks involving continuous relationships and categories of natural images.

Both humans and models identify relevant image features within a few trials. Training dataset size emerges as a major determinant of alignment with human choices. Among publicly available models that predict human generalization, contrastive training using both text and images is a common feature. The relationship between representation dimensionality and human alignment differs across model types.

The authors also evaluate three sets of representations described as human-aligned, finding no consistent predictive improvement over the baselines. Their broader conclusion is that pretrained networks appear to capture some aspects of cognition that transfer between tasks, making them useful sources of representations for cognitive models. The study also provides tasks and a modeling approach for measuring human-model alignment with natural images.
neurips-2024-evaluating-alignment-betwee.tldr: Comparing 86 pretrained models with human image learning links alignment to training data scale and identifies multimodal contrastive training as a common feature of predictive models.

paragraphs: Advanced image generators may expose an API while keeping their weights and training data private. EvolveDirector investigates whether their generated text-image pairs can train a comparable model using publicly available resources. The authors find that this can approximate an advanced model's capabilities, but straightforward training requires ten million or more samples.

That volume makes data generation costly in API fees, computation, and time. EvolveDirector uses a pretrained vision-language model to evaluate the base generator continuously and revise its training data. The revisions involve discrimination, expansion, deletion, and mutation, allowing the dataset to evolve alongside the model instead of remaining a fixed collection.

Experiments show that this process substantially reduces the required data volume. When learning from multiple advanced generators, the framework can select their best samples to develop strong, balanced capabilities. The final model, Edgen, is demonstrated to outperform those advanced models. The contribution centers on directing synthetic-data selection and revision throughout training to make learning from API-accessible generators more efficient.
neurips-2024-evolvedirector-approaching-.tldr: EvolveDirector uses a vision-language model to continually refine synthetic training data, reducing the samples needed to learn from advanced image generators.

paragraphs: Neural-network outputs used for decision making may need to obey bounds and linear constraints. GLinSAT is a layer designed to enforce these requirements on a batch of outputs. The paper treats the adjustment of network predictions as an optimization problem that can remain connected to network training.

The authors formulate output projection as entropy-regularized linear programming. Using duality, they transform it into an equivalent unconstrained convex problem with a Lipschitz-continuous gradient. They solve that formulation using accelerated gradient descent with numerical enhancements. All operations are differentiable and avoid matrix factorization; the authors describe this combination as a first for general linear satisfiability layers.

Training can propagate derivatives through automatic differentiation or through an alternative based on implicitly differentiating the optimality condition. Experiments cover constrained traveling salesman problems, graph matching with outliers, portfolio allocation, and power system unit commitment. The reported advantages over existing layers support this optimization-based design as a way to integrate linear feasibility requirements into neural-network systems.
neurips-2024-glinsat-the-general-linear-.tldr: GLinSAT enforces bounds and general linear constraints through a differentiable optimization layer that avoids matrix factorization.

paragraphs: Neural networks that process surfaces depend on how those surfaces are represented at their input. The paper argues that recent work has concentrated heavily on network architecture, sometimes giving less attention to the representation or adopting elaborate representations whose essential geometric content is difficult to interpret.

The authors propose using curvature as the input representation. Curvature describes how a surface bends and provides information about its geometry and shape. They investigate this idea through experiments using the shape operator, placing an established mathematical description of surfaces at the center of the learning pipeline. The key question is whether a more informative geometric input can improve surface processing.

Their experiments report substantial performance improvements for both segmentation and classification, together with much lower computational overhead than current methods. The findings highlight representation choice as a meaningful source of improvement alongside architecture design. In the evaluated tasks, curvature provides useful surface information without the computational burden associated with the compared approaches.
neurips-2024-improving-neural-network-su.tldr: Using curvature as a neural-network input improves surface segmentation and classification in the reported experiments while reducing computational overhead.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting represents a scene with Gaussian elements and can render new viewpoints quickly at high quality. Fitting a scene may nevertheless produce many elements, increasing memory use. Existing pruning approaches require a chosen removal ratio or importance threshold, and tuning that choice for each scene can require repeated training.

LP-3DGS makes pruning part of learning. It applies a trainable binary mask to importance scores so that the system can find a favorable pruning ratio automatically. This moves a scene-specific decision into the training process, aiming to reduce the burden of manually searching for how much of the representation can be removed.

Because a binary mask poses a gradient-computation challenge, the authors redesign the masking function using Gumbel-Sigmoid instead of the traditional straight-through estimator. The resulting formulation is differentiable and compatible with existing 3DGS training. Extensive experiments report a consistently good balance between efficiency and rendering quality, supporting learned pruning as a practical way to reduce representation size.
neurips-2024-lp-3dgs-learning-to-prune-3.tldr: LP-3DGS learns which Gaussian elements to prune during training, automatically balancing efficiency with rendering quality.

paragraphs: Confidence intervals can convey excessive certainty when a theoretical approximation neglects an error that remains substantial in actual data. The paper examines this problem in high-dimensional regression. In particular, debiased LASSO separates estimation error into a Gaussian component and a bias component that vanishes asymptotically, but the latter may still matter in finite-dimensional settings.

The authors develop a data-driven adjustment that explicitly accounts for this remaining bias. They estimate the bias terms' means and variances from training data, using high-dimensional concentration phenomena. These estimates support confidence intervals that do not depend on simply treating the bias as negligible in an asymptotic limit.

The analysis covers a broad class of predictors, extending beyond sparse regression methods to neural networks. Its significance is therefore both statistical and practical: uncertainty estimates can reflect a source of error that conventional intervals may understate. The authors identify MRI diagnosis as an application where avoiding overstated certainty could matter, and connect the framework to more reliable model-based deep learning.
neurips-2024-non-asymptotic-uncertainty-.tldr: The paper constructs non-asymptotic confidence intervals by estimating residual bias, extending uncertainty correction from sparse regression to neural-network predictors.

paragraphs: Video-forgery detectors have often focused on manipulated faces. Diffusion models can generate videos containing much broader subject matter, so a detector designed around facial forgeries may miss other synthetic content. MM-Det addresses detection across this wider range of video semantics.

The method builds a multimodal forgery representation using the representation space of a large multimodal model. This draws on the model's perceptual and broader understanding capabilities to improve detection of previously unseen forgery content. An additional attention mechanism processes information within frames and across frames, enriching features with both spatial and temporal information. A dynamic fusion strategy refines the representations as they are combined.

The authors also introduce Diffusion Video Forensics, a dataset covering a wide range of diffusion-generated forgery videos. MM-Det achieves state-of-the-art performance on this dataset. Together, the detector and dataset expand evaluation beyond the facial-manipulation focus of earlier systems, while the reported result supports combining multimodal representations with information about video structure.
neurips-2024-on-learning-multi-modal-for.tldr: MM-Det combines multimodal forgery representations with within-frame and across-frame attention, achieving state-of-the-art results on the new DVF dataset.

paragraphs: Active learning and data subset selection seek to use training examples efficiently. This paper studies stochastic gradient descent when examples are sampled according to their loss or uncertainty. Its questions concern both convergence speed and how many data samples these training procedures require.

For constant-step-size updates, the authors establish convergence results for linear classifiers on linearly separable datasets using squared hinge loss and related losses. They also extend the analysis to more general classifiers and datasets, examining a broad range of loss-based sampling strategies under smooth convex training losses. These conditions define the settings in which the theoretical conclusions apply.

The paper introduces Adaptive-Weight Sampling, or AWS, which combines sampling with an adaptive step size. Its update achieves the stochastic Polyak step size in expectation, and the authors prove convergence rates for smooth convex losses. Numerical experiments using either exact or estimated losses demonstrate efficiency across various datasets. The work connects example selection and update size through both analysis and an implementable algorithm.
neurips-2024-on-the-convergence-of-loss-.tldr: The paper analyzes loss- and uncertainty-based sampling for SGD and introduces AWS with convergence guarantees under smooth convex losses.

paragraphs: In decentralized optimization, multiple workers compute stochastic gradients and exchange information through a communication network. When both activities are asynchronous, workers can proceed at different rates. This paper studies the time required for optimization in that setting, accounting for computation and communication rather than considering updates alone.

The authors establish new lower bounds for homogeneous and heterogeneous setups under the assumption that computation and communication speeds are bounded by constants. Such bounds describe a limit on achievable time complexity within the studied setting. They provide a reference against which an algorithm's efficiency can be judged.

The paper then introduces Fragile SGD, described as nearly optimal, and Amelie SGD, described as optimal. The methods converge with arbitrary heterogeneous computation and communication speeds and match the derived lower bounds, allowing a logarithmic factor in the homogeneous setting. Their theoretical time complexities improve on previous synchronous and asynchronous stochastic methods in the decentralized setup. The contribution pairs performance limits with algorithms that approach or attain those limits.
neurips-2024-on-the-optimal-time-complex.tldr: The paper derives decentralized asynchronous optimization time bounds and introduces Fragile SGD and Amelie SGD to approach or match them.

paragraphs: In-context learning adapts a language model by placing example inputs and labels in its prompt. Performance depends on which examples are chosen and how they are ordered. EASE addresses both decisions while also recognizing that the surrounding instruction can influence how useful the examples are.

The method represents ordered example sets using hidden embeddings from a pretrained language model. A neural bandit algorithm then searches for an effective ordered set. Instead of retrieving a new set for each test query, EASE finds one set intended to perform well across queries from the same task, removing the need for selection computation at test time.

The framework can also jointly optimize the instruction and examples. Extensive empirical evaluations, including novel tasks, show advantages over existing methods and provide insights into how example selection affects in-context learning. The central contribution is to treat prompt examples as an ordered collection to optimize, with a reusable task-level result and an extension that accounts for instruction choice.
neurips-2024-prompt-optimization-with-ea.tldr: EASE uses neural bandit optimization to select reusable, ordered prompt examples and can jointly optimize the accompanying instruction.

paragraphs: Radiotherapy planning adjusts radiation beam shapes and intensities to treat a tumor while limiting exposure to healthy tissue. This requires solving large constrained optimization problems within clinical time limits. A large matrix sits at the center of the computation, making its storage and processing important practical concerns.

A common shortcut removes small matrix entries to make the matrix sparse. The paper explains that this approximation can reduce treatment-plan quality, potentially increasing healthy-tissue exposure or leaving the tumor inadequately irradiated. The authors investigate randomized sketching as a way to obtain a sparse representation while preserving the information needed for planning.

They demonstrate that randomized sketch tools can sparsify the matrix without sacrificing treatment quality in their study. They also develop a new randomized sketch method with theoretical guarantees that outperforms existing techniques in practical application. The contribution connects a matrix-compression method to a concrete planning requirement: reducing computational burden while retaining the quality of the resulting treatment plan.
neurips-2024-randomized-sparse-matrix-co.tldr: Randomized matrix sparsification reduces the computational burden of radiotherapy optimization while preserving treatment quality in the reported study.

paragraphs: Teaching a robot through reinforcement learning requires a reward that identifies useful behavior. Designing that reward by hand can be laborious. Expert videos offer another source of guidance: a robot's trajectory can be compared with a demonstrated trajectory, and their alignment can provide a proxy reward.

Optimal transport has been used to measure this alignment, including work learning from only one or a few demonstrations. The paper identifies a problem with earlier formulations: their reward does not change with temporal order. Consequently, the reward can overlook information about the sequence of behavior, potentially introducing noise into the learning signal.

TemporalOT incorporates temporal order into the optimal-transport reward to make the proxy signal more accurate. The method therefore uses information about when events occur as part of comparing robot behavior with expert demonstrations. Extensive experiments on Meta-world benchmark tasks validate its efficacy. The contribution is a targeted improvement to demonstration-derived rewards that addresses a specific source of ambiguity in trajectory alignment.
neurips-2024-robot-policy-learning-with-.tldr: TemporalOT incorporates temporal order into optimal-transport rewards, improving the learning signal derived from expert robot demonstrations.

paragraphs: Training losses involving high-order derivatives can become expensive as both input dimension and derivative order increase. The derivative tensor grows with dimension, while ordinary backpropagation also faces rapid growth in its computation graph. Earlier work addressed these difficulties separately through randomized computation and high-order automatic differentiation.

The paper connects those approaches. By constructing suitable input tangents for univariate high-order automatic differentiation, the authors efficiently compute arbitrary contractions of multivariate derivative tensors at arbitrary order. These contractions combine derivative entries in specified ways, allowing the method to randomize differential operators without explicitly processing the entire tensor through the earlier approach.

Applied to physics-informed neural networks, the method reports more than a thousandfold speedup and over thirtyfold memory reduction compared with randomization using first-order automatic differentiation. The authors also report solving million-dimensional partial differential equations in eight minutes on one NVIDIA A100 GPU. These results support the possibility of using high-order differential operators in substantially larger learning problems.
neurips-2024-stochastic-taylor-derivativ.tldr: The estimator combines randomized derivative computation with high-order automatic differentiation, yielding major reported speed and memory gains for physics-informed neural networks.

paragraphs: Weak supervision builds training labels from inexpensive but imperfect sources, often expressed as labeling functions. Its practical value is difficult to assess because results depend on the data, those functions, how their outputs are combined, and the final model. Simplistic tasks or poorly constructed functions can therefore give a misleading impression of the approach.

BOXWRENCH is a benchmark designed around more realistic uses of weak supervision. Its tasks include more classes and class imbalance, meaningful requirements for domain expertise, and opportunities to reuse labeling functions across parallel multilingual collections. The authors also use a careful procedure for writing the functions, aiming to better reflect how they would be developed in practice.

On this benchmark, ordinary supervised learning needs more than a thousand labeled examples to match weak supervision in many settings. The result suggests that weak supervision's value can look substantially different when evaluation includes realistic task demands and thoughtfully written labeling functions. It is a finding about many evaluated settings rather than a universal sample requirement.
neurips-2024-stronger-than-you-think-ben.tldr: BOXWRENCH finds that supervised learning needs over a thousand labeled examples to match weak supervision in many realistic benchmark settings.

paragraphs: Describing spatial relationships in an image and generating an image from a spatial description are closely related tasks. Both require understanding a scene's three-dimensional structure. This paper proposes learning them together so that information useful in one direction can help the other.

The authors introduce a shared 3D scene graph representation for spatial features. Their Spatial Dual Discrete Diffusion framework uses the observation that producing an image or text from a 3D representation is easier than inferring that representation from an image or text. Intermediate features from the easier directions guide learning in the harder directions, connecting the two generation tasks through their shared scene structure.

On the VSD visual spatial understanding dataset, the system significantly outperforms mainstream text-to-image and image-to-text methods. Further analysis examines the contribution of the dual learning strategy. The findings support coordinating the two tasks around a common spatial representation, with guidance flowing between complementary generation processes to improve spatial understanding in both directions.
neurips-2024-synergistic-dual-spatial-aw.tldr: The framework jointly learns spatial image-to-text and text-to-image generation through a shared 3D scene graph and mutually supporting learning processes.

paragraphs: An experiment may influence a variable of interest without directly controlling it or removing confounding influences. With high-dimensional measurements and nonlinear mechanisms, these indirect interventions generally do not identify a unique answer to a causal question. The paper focuses on making experiments informative even when that ambiguity remains.

The authors develop an adaptive strategy that chooses experiments to narrow the gap between upper and lower bounds on a targeted query. Instead of requiring complete recovery of the underlying mechanism, the strategy concentrates on the particular scientific question being asked. Each experimental choice contributes to progressively tightening the range of answers compatible with the analysis.

The general framework involves a two-level optimization procedure. For causal effects, the authors derive an analytical kernel-based estimator that makes the bounds efficiently estimable. They demonstrate efficacy in synthetic settings combining confounding, multiple variables, and nonlinear relationships. The contribution turns unresolved causal identification into a sequential design objective: reduce the remaining uncertainty about a specific query through carefully chosen indirect experiments.
neurips-2024-targeted-sequential-indirec.tldr: The method adaptively selects indirect experiments to tighten bounds on a targeted causal query when confounding prevents unique identification.

paragraphs: A vision encoder that recognizes natural images well may struggle to recognize text. UNIT trains one encoder to support both capabilities. It begins with an image-pretrained encoder and introduces a lightweight language decoder for text prediction alongside a lightweight vision decoder intended to preserve the encoder's existing image capabilities.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, the model learns unified representations from images and documents at their commonly used resolutions. It then trains on scale-exchanged data, where images and documents appear at less typical resolutions. This second stage targets robustness to changes in scale, connecting recognition ability with the resolution at which content is presented.

UNIT retains the original vision encoder architecture, so the framework adds no inference or deployment cost to that encoder. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show substantial improvements on document tasks, including optical character recognition and document question answering, while maintaining natural-image performance. The findings support a training-based route to broader visual recognition without sacrificing the encoder's original image capabilities.
neurips-2024-unit-unifying-image-and-tex.tldr: UNIT trains a single unchanged vision encoder for image and text recognition, improving document tasks while maintaining natural-image performance.

paragraphs: Word embeddings occupy an uneven geometric space, and adjusting that geometry can improve language-task performance. The paper identifies a mismatch in many existing approaches: they implicitly treat words as equally frequent, even though actual language contains a few very common words and many rare ones, following Zipf's law.

The proposed correction is PCA whitening weighted by observed word frequency. The authors report that this simple change substantially improves task performance and surpasses established baselines. Their theoretical account distinguishes methods according to whether the probability model underlying word representations uses a uniform or Zipfian base measure.

Using the Zipfian formulation naturally gives informative low-frequency words greater emphasis through their vector norms. The authors connect this explanation to information geometry and losses for imbalanced classification. Their theory also supports an explanation for the effectiveness of several existing language methods: those methods encode empirical word frequency in their underlying probabilistic models. The contribution links a practical geometric adjustment to a frequency-aware account of representation quality.
neurips-2024-zipfian-whitening-527951d04.tldr: Frequency-weighted PCA whitening improves word-embedding performance, with a theory connecting representation geometry to the unequal frequencies of words.
